analysis.one_liner: Makes estate tax repeal permanent and expands immediate equipment deductions for small businesses.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently eliminated the federal estate tax, which under the 2001 tax law was scheduled to come back in 2011, and made related gift-tax reductions permanent [S2]. It also would have roughly eight-fold increased the amount of equipment small businesses can deduct immediately rather than over years, raised the phaseout to $800,000, kept computer software eligible, and let self-employed people deduct health insurance costs when calculating self-employment taxes [S2]. The estate tax repeal was by far the largest and most concentrated piece: it applies only to the largest estates in the country. The bill never received a hearing or a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates gain the most, since permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping taxes would eliminate a tax that in 2009 applied only above a multi-million-dollar exemption and falls on well under one percent of estates. Small business owners gain from the larger immediate deduction for equipment and software purchases, and self-employed people gain from deducting health insurance premiums against self-employment tax. Estate planning and wealth-advisory work for large estates would remain a growth business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs to the largest estates; small business owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make permanent the repeal of the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax and the gift-tax reductions enacted in the 2001 tax law, which were otherwise scheduled to expire after 2010 [S2].

It would raise the small business 'Section 179' expensing allowance from $25,000 to $200,000, raise the phaseout threshold to $800,000, add inflation adjustments, keep computer software eligible, and make the election revocable permanently [S2].
It would let self-employed people deduct health insurance costs in computing net self-employment income for payroll-tax purposes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury pays, meaning either future taxpayers or the programs that would have been funded with that revenue. The estate tax repeal is the dominant cost because it permanently removes revenue that comes almost entirely from the wealthiest households in the country; the expanded expensing and health deduction add smaller revenue losses. Public services and programs backed by general revenue bear the cost in the long run.

drawbacks.text: Permanent estate tax repeal is the bill's largest and most concentrated provision: the estate tax in that era applied only to the biggest estates, so the revenue forgone flows overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households while the bill's title emphasizes family farms and small businesses [S2].
Making permanent full repeal of the estate tax removes a progressive revenue source permanently, adding to deficits that eventually must be paid for through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts.

The expanded expensing, while useful to businesses making real equipment purchases, is a broadened business tax break that also reduces federal revenue; its benefits scale with how much a business spends on new assets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The small-business expensing and self-employed health-deduction pieces are conventional, defensible tax provisions with modest costs. The estate tax repeal is a different matter: it is a permanent, very large tax cut aimed at the largest estates in the country, and its revenue cost dwarfs the other provisions. Bundling the two under a 'family farms' title does not change that the dominant effect is eliminating a tax on concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Randy Neugebauer introduced the bill on January 14, 2009 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax was not permanently repealed through this route, and the federal revenue it raises from the largest estates remained on the books in some form. The self-employed and small-business provisions also never took effect, so no one gained those benefits either; the clearest winners are federal revenues and the programs they support, rather than any lobby.

for.name: Randy Neugebauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill making estate tax repeal and small-business expensing permanent; secured no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 14, 2009 and took no further action; the bill never reached a hearing or floor vote.

against.name: Charlie Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for consideration in the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican with zero cosponsors of either party and received no votes, so the partisan shape can only be read from inaction: the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee and House majority never moved it.

industries.note: Permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping taxes would eliminate a tax that applies only to the largest estates, delivering the bill's biggest benefit to the richest families. The cost is forgone federal revenue that other taxpayers or programs would otherwise not have to cover.

The bill raises the immediate expensing allowance for equipment and software from $25,000 to $200,000 and raises the phaseout to $800,000, letting smaller firms deduct purchases now instead of over years and freeing cash flow.
The bill lets self-employed people deduct health insurance costs in calculating self-employment tax, closing a gap where employees avoid that tax on employer-paid premiums.
